data.description:
## Summary

`scripts/check_orphaned_load.py` exits **1** on `/Applications/Caffeine.app`, a long-running user
GUI application that no agent or investigation spawned. Because the script is the sanctioned
"did I leak processes?" check that AGENTS.md points every agent at, a persistent false positive
means it cannot be used as a clean pass/fail gate.

```
check_orphaned_load: 1 orphaned process(es) with PPID 1 above 3600 CPU-seconds (11 system-owned suppressed):
  pid=1159     cpu=      3636.4s (1.0h)
    /Applications/Caffeine.app/Contents/MacOS/Caffeine
```

Exit code 1. The advisory text then instructs the reader to *"confirm the owning investigation is
over, then terminate them"* — advice that is actively wrong here, since terminating it would kill
the operator's desktop app.

## Three independent observations in one session (2026-09-05)

- An agent investigating the Gerrit 504s: *"The one non-system orphan is `Caffeine.app`, a
  pre-existing desktop utility (1.0h CPU, not spawned by this session)."*
- An agent working the duplicate-ticket RCA: *"`check_orphaned_load.py` exits 1, but its sole
  non-system finding is `/Applications/Caffeine.app` ... I'd rather report that honestly than kill
  someone's app to make a checker green."*
- The orchestrator, independently, on the same host.

Each had to investigate the finding, satisfy themselves it was not theirs, and explain it in a
handoff. That is the cost: three separate parties spending attention, and a standing incentive to
either ignore a nonzero exit (dangerous — it is the only leak signal) or kill a user's application
to get a green (worse).

## Why the existing suppression does not cover it

The script already suppresses 11 system-owned orphans as launchd-parented by design. `Caffeine.app`
is not system-owned by that test — it is a user application in `/Applications` that launchd
reparents to PID 1 like any other detached GUI process. The classifier's notion of "system-owned"
does not include "user GUI application", so a whole category of legitimate long-lived processes
falls through into the leak bucket.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)

Options, roughly in order of preference:
1. Treat processes whose executable lives under `/Applications` (or carries a `.app` bundle path) as
   not-agent-spawned, in the same class as the existing system-owned suppression.
2. Bound the check to processes started SINCE the session began, or under a known scratch/worktree
   path — a leak this script cares about is one the current work created, and CPU-seconds alone
   cannot distinguish that from a legitimate long-running app.
3. An explicit allowlist. Weakest — it needs maintaining and the next GUI app repeats this.

Whatever is chosen, the exit code must still go nonzero for a REAL leak; option 2 is attractive
precisely because it narrows on provenance rather than on identity.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 A long-running user GUI application does not produce a nonzero exit.
- [ ] AC2 A genuine leaked helper (the `while True: pass` shape the script exists to catch) STILL
      produces a nonzero exit and is named. Prove both branches, not just the changed one.
- [ ] AC3 The advisory text does not instruct the reader to terminate a process the script should
      not have flagged.

## Constraints

Never use `--force` or any gate bypass. `timeout` does not exist on this macOS host (exit 127) —
bound with `perl -e 'alarm N; exec @ARGV'`. Do not touch the shared main checkout; do not
`git stash` anywhere.
data.title: check_orphaned_load.py exits 1 on a user GUI app, so the leak gate cannot be trusted green
